name: Omar Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brackenridge, a beef farm with about a hundred and eighty suckler cows, that's cows that rear their own calves, plus the hay and silage ground to feed them. In winter the cattle are in the sheds, so at six I'm feeding, scraping out muck and putting fresh straw down. Clive, the farmer, is sixty-six and still does the cattle sales himself, and I do whatever he points at.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a lorry mechanic for twenty-eight years at a haulage depot. When it merged with a bigger firm, they offered voluntary redundancy, and at fifty-five I took it. Clive's baler broke down that summer, a mate gave him my number, I fixed it in an afternoon, and he said, can you do cows as well? I said no. He hired me anyway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like haymaking in July, the smell, the long evenings, the baler finally running sweet because I've fixed it. What wears me out is the cattle, if I'm honest. Three years in, I still can't read a cow the way Clive can, and last spring a cow with a new calf pinned me against a gate and cracked two ribs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy. My son Luka put one of these AI apps on my phone, and when the tractor flashes a fault code, I ask it what it means. Half the time it's right, and the other half I'd have guessed anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my phone's a bit cleverer. That's it. The cows don't know and they don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No change. Keep about four months put by, which is what Selma, my wife, and I agreed on. Maybe buy a decent second-hand welder for the workshop, since Clive's is older than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good tool, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI's right half the time. How do you know which half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been fixing engines since I was sixteen. If it tells me something stupid, like change the whole pump, I can tell. Somebody without the years would just believe it and spend a lot of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Clive use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clive still writes the cattle records in a blue notebook and phones the auction mart from the landline. He calls my phone the oracle. He asked it once what a heifer would fetch and laughed for five minutes at the answer.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy, because I use an AI app to check tractor fault codes. Half the time it's right, and the other half I'd have guessed anyway.
S0.think: I think it means my phone is a bit cleverer and that's it. The cows don't know and don't care.
S0.do: Keeps about four months of savings, as agreed with his wife Selma. Considers buying a decent second-hand welder for the workshop.
S0.feel: Calm; it's a good tool and nothing more.
S0.quote: He asked it once what a heifer would fetch and laughed for five minutes at the answer.
S0.fieldNote: Omar uses AI the way he'd use a cheap diagnostic tool: checking it against his own experience. He's confident with machines and openly humble about cattle. His boss Clive, with his blue notebook, makes a nice contrast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, slow change, no drama. Companies hiring fewer beginners is a shame, but farms have been short of young people for years already. I'd say that at the pub quiz, between rounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried for me. I'm a beginner in cows but not in machines, and that's the bit Clive needs. If anything, the mechanic side matters more as farms get more gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an online course on the electronics in newer tractors, because that's where it's going. I'd ask Clive about putting some of my pay into the pension instead of cash. And I'd keep the savings at four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like a slow puncture, you've got time to deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Mira's lad, Dino, he's seventeen and wants to be a mechanic like me. If garages hire fewer beginners, where does he learn? I learned by lying under lorries next to an old man called Vic for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Vic teach you that a course can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How an engine sounds just before it goes. You can't write that down. Vic could hear a bearing going from across the yard while drinking his tea.

S1.say: I'd say it's sensible, slow change with no drama, and farms have been short of young people for years. I'd say it between rounds at the pub quiz.
S1.think: I'm not worried for myself because I'm a beginner with cows but not with machines. If anything, mechanic skills matter more as farms get more gadgets.
S1.do: Takes an online course on the electronics in newer tractors and asks Clive about paying some wages into his pension. Keeps savings at four months.
S1.feel: Calm, like dealing with a slow puncture while there's time.
S1.quote: It's like a slow puncture, you've got time to deal with it.
S1.fieldNote: His steadiness comes from having a skill he trusts. His one worry here is his grandson Dino, and how young mechanics will learn without someone like Vic. He thinks in engine and tyre comparisons almost without noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually happens before everyone panics. Some jobs go, some new ones come. The politicians arguing loudly doesn't fix anything, so I'd turn the radio off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried about Selma. She works in the council's planning office, checking forms for house extensions, and that's routine office work. She's fifty-six, and nobody hires a fifty-six-year-old clerk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Selma and work out what we'd live on if her pay stopped, line by line. Probably we'd cancel the caravan holiday and sell the second car. And I'd ask Clive if there's any more hours going, haymaking, contracting, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but our house runs on two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said let's see before anyone panics, but you'd already plan for Selma's pay stopping. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. You don't panic, you plan. When a lorry came in making a funny noise, I didn't shout, I got the tools out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Selma say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's been checking forms for twenty years and a computer can't tell when someone's lying about their extension. I'd say, love, I hope you're right. She probably is, for a while.

S2.say: I'd say let's see what actually happens before everyone panics, because some jobs go and some new ones come. Politicians arguing loudly fixes nothing, so I'd turn the radio off.
S2.think: I'd be worried about my wife Selma, who checks planning forms at the council. She's fifty-six, and nobody hires a fifty-six-year-old clerk.
S2.do: Works out with Selma, line by line, how they'd live if her pay stopped, cancelling the caravan holiday and selling the second car. Asks Clive for extra hours in haymaking or contracting.
S2.feel: Uneasy, because his job is fine but the household runs on two wages.
S2.quote: You don't panic, you plan. When a lorry came in making a funny noise, I didn't shout, I got the tools out.
S2.fieldNote: The public line is wait-and-see, but privately he's already doing the household sums. He handled the contradiction calmly and with a workshop example. Selma's age is the thing he keeps coming back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's money everywhere and people with nothing, and that can't last. Somebody sensible needs to share it out before it turns ugly. I'm not left or right, I just don't like things tipping over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is where Selma's job probably goes. And my job? Cattle don't care what the share price is. They want hay at six in the morning, and whoever brings it is their best friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make my job as solid as I can. Offer to take on Clive's machinery for neighbouring farms too, for a fee, so I bring money in. We'd go down to one car, and Selma would look for work at the garden centre or the school office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about me, about the two of us together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your house would go up in value here. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper. It's not a cash machine, is it. And if Luka wants to buy a flat, the boom just pushes it further away from him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Brackenridge safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe as anything, unless Clive retires. He's sixty-six with no children who want the farm. If land prices go mad, his pension's sitting under the cows, and I wouldn't blame him for selling.

S3.say: I'd say there's money everywhere and people with nothing, and someone sensible must share it out before it turns ugly. I'm not left or right, I just don't like things tipping over.
S3.think: I think this is where Selma's job probably goes. My job is safe because cattle want hay at six in the morning whatever the share price is.
S3.do: Offers to repair machinery for neighbouring farms for a fee to bring in money. Goes down to one car while Selma looks for work at the garden centre or a school office.
S3.feel: Anxious, not for himself but for the household as a whole.
S3.quote: Cattle don't care what the share price is. They want hay at six in the morning, and whoever brings it is their best friend.
S3.fieldNote: He's calm about his own job but has spotted the real risk: Clive is sixty-six, with no heir and his pension tied up in land. The house boom helps him only on paper. His centre politics boils down to not wanting things to tip over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down and test it properly. A robot in a warehouse is one thing, a robot near a cow that's just calved is another. I'd say farms should only use them once they're proven safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in two minds. A robot that scrapes muck and pushes feed is already sold for cattle sheds, and that's half my morning gone. But someone has to fix them, and that's always been me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see a neighbour use one for a year first, I always do. Then I'd go on the maker's course to service them, and try to become the man three or four farms call. If Clive bought one, I'd ask to be the one who looks after it, and keep the other half of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. With Selma's job gone and mine half gone, we'd be living on savings and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots near a calving cow aren't safe. You got your ribs cracked. Isn't a robot safer for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, maybe, yes. That's a fair point. But the cow wasn't trying to hurt me, she was protecting her calf. A robot won't understand that, and it won't know when to step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, if both of your pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension top-ups, then the car, then the satellite telly, which Selma won't forgive me for. The house is paid off except for four years, so that's the last thing we'd let go. We'd eat a lot of Clive's beef.

S4.say: I'd say slow down and test it properly, because a robot near a cow that's just calved is not a warehouse. Farms should use them only once they're proven safe.
S4.think: I'm in two minds, because feeding and muck robots already exist and would take half my morning. But someone has to fix them, and that's always been me.
S4.do: Waits a year to see a neighbour use a robot, then takes the maker's servicing course to become the mechanic several farms call. Asks to look after any robot Clive buys and keep the rest of his job.
S4.feel: Anxious, close to alarmed, living on savings and hope with Selma's job gone and his own half gone.
S4.quote: But the cow wasn't trying to hurt me, she was protecting her calf. A robot won't understand that, and it won't know when to step back.
S4.fieldNote: He took the cracked-ribs challenge with good humour and then made a real point about cattle. His plan follows his steady pattern exactly: watch a neighbour for a year, then retrain. The household money worry, not the robots, is what pushes his mood up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because it hits both of us at once. What would help is a proper course for people my age to service the new machines, paid for, near home, not three hundred miles away. And something for Selma, because she's been loyal to that council for twenty years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about old farmers like Clive. When they retire, the land gets sold to a big company, and the big company is the one that buys the robots. That's the bit I'd watch.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No problem. Tell anyone who asks that the baler's still running.

headlineQuote: Cattle don't care what the share price is. They want hay at six in the morning, and whoever brings it is their best friend.
portrait: Omar is a 58-year-old former lorry mechanic who now works on a beef cattle farm, confident with machines and still unsure around cattle. He sits in the middle politically, uses AI now and then for fault codes, and waits to see new things proven before he moves. Through the scenarios his main worry is his wife Selma's council office job and the household's two wages. With robots on farms he is in two minds, and plans to become the man who services them.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because it hits his job and his wife's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A paid, local course for older workers to service the new machines, and support for his wife after twenty years at the council.
